questions.prompt: What pressure does Chapter 4 say norms create for selfish actors?
choices: They create pressure to get the benefit of cheating without paying the full cost of open violation
They remove selfish incentives entirely
They make every violation impossible to hide

explanation.gentle: The chapter says rules change how selfishness is pursued, not whether the motive disappears.
explanation.direct: Norms make actors search for gain under cover.
explanation.competitive: The game becomes payoff plus deniability.

questions.prompt: What makes the chapter's most interesting cases of cheating distinctive?
choices: They happen only in perfect secrecy
They occur in broad daylight with thin cover
They depend on formal court rulings

explanation.gentle: The chapter emphasizes violations people can often see but struggle to punish.
explanation.direct: Its central cases are public cheating under ambiguity.

questions.prompt: What is a thin fig leaf doing in the chapter's framework?
choices: It makes the violation harder to prosecute by raising the cost of confrontation
It proves nobody noticed the violation
It turns a norm into a formal law

explanation.gentle: The cover does not need to be strong if it makes pushing the case harder.
explanation.direct: Its function is burden-shifting, not perfect persuasion.
explanation.competitive: The excuse works by making the hit costly.

questions.prompt: A coworker bends a policy in public and immediately offers a flimsy explanation that makes everyone hesitate to object. Which chapter idea best explains the hesitation?
choices: The norm has disappeared completely
A thin fig leaf has made escalation socially costly
People no longer care about proof

explanation.gentle: The excuse is buying hesitation more than belief.
explanation.direct: The cover protects the violation by making accusation awkward and effortful.
explanation.competitive: The room stalls because the case just got more expensive.

questions.prompt: A team sees a player break a rule, but no one speaks first because nobody knows who will back them. What concept is most visible?
choices: The common knowledge problem
The disappearance of competition
A failure of all norms everywhere

explanation.gentle: The problem is not that people failed to notice. It is that they could not coordinate their certainty.
explanation.direct: Common knowledge matters when enforcement requires visible backing.
explanation.competitive: The room saw it and still could not line up.

choices: Cheating only matters when it is completely secret
Excuses can shape enforcement
Groups may avoid confrontation

explanation.gentle: The chapter says public cheating under cover is one of the most important cases.
explanation.direct: Its target is the hidden-only picture of norm violation.
explanation.competitive: The public cheat is part of the main story, not a side case.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 4 grow out of Chapter 3 on norms?
choices: Norms create incentives to seek selfish gains under ambiguous cover
Norms make all selfish motives vanish
Norms matter only when formal punishments are certain

explanation.gentle: Once rules exist, people may try to keep the gain while avoiding the social penalty.
explanation.direct: Cheating becomes the next move under norm pressure.

questions.prompt: A committee dislikes a violation but avoids gathering evidence or confronting the violator because the process would be exhausting and awkward. What chapter mechanism is that?
choices: Perfect enforcement
Enforcement laziness and cost avoidance
Proof that the rule has no supporters

explanation.gentle: The chapter says rules can fail because enforcement takes effort people would rather avoid.
explanation.direct: Private disapproval is easier than proof work and escalation.
explanation.competitive: The room hates the hassle more than it hates the move.

questions.prompt: Why can cheating survive even when many observers are not fooled by the excuse?
choices: Because only full belief can support cheating
Because ambiguity can still block shared proof and coordinated action
Because broad support for the rule is impossible

explanation.gentle: The cover does not need believers if it keeps the case from becoming clean and public.
explanation.direct: The chapter's mechanism is hesitation under evidential and social friction, not universal deception.
explanation.competitive: The lie can lose the argument and still win the round.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest bridge from Chapter 4 into Chapter 5 on self-deception?
choices: Once public cover stops working, people stop cheating
If excuses can hide motives from others, the mind may help hide them inwardly too
Self-deception matters only when norms disappear

explanation.gentle: The next step is concealment moving from social cover into the actor's own mind.
explanation.direct: Self-deception extends the cheating logic inward.
explanation.competitive: The next fig leaf grows inside the player.
